newsitem.title: UK: Chairman quits UK lobby firm in "sleaze" row.
newsitem.headline: Chairman quits UK lobby firm in "sleaze" row.

text.p: The head of a British lobbying firm at the centre of a row over parliamentary sleaze wracking the ruling Conservative Party announced his resignation in Monday's edition of the Times.
Ian Greer, chairman of Ian Greer Associates (IGA), said in an interview with the daily: "I decided for the sake and honour of my clients, who have stayed loyal to me, to stand aside."
"It was difficult. I was proud of IGA. It is still viable, but I knew the name Greer had to go."

IGA is caught up in in a scandal over cash payments to members of parliament in return for their tabling questions in the House of Commons. The affair has gravely embarrassed the ruling Conservative Party of Prime Minister John Major.
Greer said in his interview that he had raised 750,000 pounds ($1.17 million) for the Conservatives over the past decade.
"It seemed the right thing to do. I regret now being so enthusiastic," he said.
Greer said he was paid to provide a car and offices for Major's 1990 party leadership campaign and that ministers had approached him for help with their election expenses.
Earlier, the three directors of IGA's Brussels-based subsidiary and two British-based directors announced they were quitting.
Brad Staples, managing director of Ian Greer Europe, said he and fellow directors Liam McArthur and Edward Walsh had been kept in the dark about the London office's activities.

Confirming the resignations, Staples told Reuters: "The reason is that we were not fully informed of Mr Greer's financial relations with MPs in the UK. I no longer have confidence in Mr Greer's management."
Robbie MacDuff and Jonathan Hopkins, both long-time Labour Party members and trade unionists, also accused Greer of withholding information concerning the scandal from them and fellow members.
Greer and Neil Hamilton, a Conservative former minister, last week dropped a libel action against the Guardian newspaper, which had named them in connection with the cash-for-questions scandal.
The row has spiralled into a major embarrassment for the Conservatives as they prepare for their last annual conference ahead of a general election which Major must call by next May.

Hamilton is to be probed by parliament's Commissioner For Standards, Sir Gordon Downey, following claims by Mohamed Al-Fayed, owner of London's Harrods store, that he paid the MP cash to table parliamentary questions.
Hamilton has admitted accepting 10,000 pounds ($15,600) from Greer, who has also made payments to campaign funds of a number of MPs from all three main parties. Most were Conservatives.
On Thursday, Lady Turner of Camden, a member of the IGA board, was sacked as the opposition Labour Party's employment spokeswoman in the unelected House of Lords after she defended Greer's actions.
